Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

vignette: Mateo Rivera was twenty-two when he first sought help, but the war had been quietly following him home for more than a year. At twenty, he had been working as a logistics coordinator in a border city when the first mortar struck the market district. He was stacking crates in a ground-floor warehouse, the roof groaning overhead, when the impact threw him against a metal shelving unit. Dust plumed inward, metal shrieked, and the world narrowed to the pressure against his ribs and the ringing in his ears. He spent the next three days sheltering in the building’s interior hallway, pressing his palms against his sternum to feel the steady rhythm of his own heart. When evacuation finally brought him across the ocean, the shift to a quiet American city felt less like arrival and more like suspended animation. Over the following months, Mateo’s body refused to unwind. He had come to believe that the tightness spreading across his shoulders and neck was a signal that danger was still near, not merely the fatigue of travel. His body remained constantly on alert, coiled and ready to react, and he found himself perpetually watchful. In his new role as a Product Manager, where his desk faced an open corridor and his monitors streamed continuous team updates, every shift in posture or sudden pivot of a colleague sent a jolt through him. He was certain that an unexpected movement nearby meant a threat had materialized, so he began tracking the space around his workstation, his eyes never fully settling. The startle response was sharp and immediate; when a teammate dropped a tablet or a printer engaged without warning, Mateo’s breath caught and his shoulders hiked as though bracing for impact. His symptom count rested in the mid-range, yet the persistent tension kept him from feeling settled. These reactions settled into steady habits over weeks and months, existing side by side rather than chaining together. He would pinch his forearm or press a thumb hard into his wrist, using the physical hurt to release the overwhelming feelings that threatened to spill over. Alongside this, he kept asking others to reassure him that he was okay. In sprint reviews and hallway conversations, he would pause mid-sentence to ask his analysts whether he looked pale, whether his breathing sounded normal, whether everything was alright. The body monitoring grew equally persistent; he would constantly check his body for signs of danger or injury, running a hand over his ribs, flexing his fingers against his thighs, pressing his palms to his temples as though verifying that nothing had broken or hidden. The warehouse’s metal groans still echoed in his mind whenever the conference room door swung open, a quiet reminder of what had first broken his stillness. The accumulation of these patterns altered his daily rhythm. His Product Manager responsibilities demanded constant coordination, yet his hypervigilance and startle responses made the open office feel exposed. He began arriving early to clear the glass-walled conference room, avoiding the rush of footsteps and sudden gestures that triggered his reactions. Colleagues adapted, but a quiet distance settled over his interactions. He was single, and though he wanted to connect, he often declined evening plans, telling himself he was simply conserving energy. What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday stand-up when a project lead leaned in quickly to highlight a roadmap on the monitor. Mateo flinched so sharply he knocked over his water bottle, and as he apologized repeatedly, asking again and again if he had been alright, he realized the war had not ended; it had simply moved into his nervous system. He wanted to understand why his body would not let go, and he hoped to learn how to live without bracing for the next impact.
